(a) Judgment debtor who has acquired the decree: The second proviso to Rule 16 bars execution by a judgment debtor who has acquired the decree - the decree is extinguished as between him and the co-judgment debtors (AIR 1956 TC 171 FB; AIR 1943 Madras 641; AIR 1932 Allahabad 704; 5 Allahabad 27).

(b) Person who obtained the decree fraudulently: A person who obtained the decree by fraud cannot use it to execute against the judgment debtor (AIR 1939 Bombay 97; AIR 1937 Lahore 4; AIR 1931 Allahabad 549 FB; AIR 1930 Lahore 89; AIR 1929 NWFP 21).

(c) Person who did not receive proper notice under Rule 16: A person who did not receive proper notice under Rule 16 cannot execute the decree (AIR 1939 Bombay 97; AIR 1937 Lahore 4; AIR 1931 Allahabad 549 FB; AIR 1930 Lahore 89; AIR 1929 NWFP 21).

For Pakistani practitioners: always verify that the applicant has a valid basis for seeking execution - either through a valid assignment, inheritance, or appointment as receiver.

The procedure for the court to grant a sale certificate under Order XXI Rule 94 CPC 1908 involves both substantive requirements and procedural steps. Substantive Requirements: The sale certificate must specify: (i) the name of the person declared to be the purchaser at the time of the sale (Rule 94(1)(a)); (ii) the date and description of the property sold (Rule 94(1)(b)). These two elements are mandatory - the certificate must contain them. The Lahore High Court has held that the certificate must be issued in the prescribed form (Appendix E, Form No. 38) and must be signed by the presiding officer of the court (PLD 1993 L 706; 1995 CLC 1922). The certificate is issued after the court has confirmed the sale under Rule 92 - the confirmation is the prerequisite for the certificate. Procedural Steps: Step 1 - After the sale, the court records the results of the auction in the Register of Auction Sales (Form No. 37). Step 2 - The court then issues the sale certificate under Rule 94 to the confirmed purchaser. Step 3 - The certificate is served on the purchaser (and the judgment debtor if applicable) and recorded in the Register of Auction Sales. Step 4 - The purchaser uses the certificate to apply for delivery of possession under Rule 95. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has emphasized that the certificate is not the source of title - it merely documents the title that already exists by virtue of the confirmed sale (PLD 2005 SC 819; 2013 CLC 1679). The certificate is not compulsorily registerable (1998 CLC 1256; 1995 CLC 1922), but it is liable to stamp duty (2002 CLD 145; 1998 CLC 1256). The certificate must be issued within the 30-day period allowed for challenging the sale under Rule 90 - if issued after the challenge period expires, the certificate will not be valid against persons who had challenged the sale. For Pakistani practitioners, the practical advice is to obtain the certificate promptly after confirmation, serve it on the purchaser, and file it in the court records.

Tariq Mahmood's combined suit for rent arrears and defamation raises the multifariousness objection under Order I Rule 8 of the CPC 1908. The court must examine whether these two causes of action are so different in nature that they should not be joined in the same suit. Analysis of the two causes of action: (a) Rent Arrears - a money recovery suit for past and future rent payments owed by the defendant tenant. This is a pure civil money claim arising from a contractual relationship (tenancy agreement). (b) Defamation - a tort claim for injury to reputation. This is a personal, non-contractual claim. Nature of the two causes of action: (i) Both are civil suits - both arise from the defendant's conduct towards Tariq Mahmood. (ii) Both involve the same defendant. (iii) Both are pending in the same court. (iv) Both arose from the same transaction sequence - the tenancy relationship. (v) Both are within the court's pecuniary jurisdiction. (vi) Both are within the court's subject matter jurisdiction. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that where two causes of action arise from the same transaction and involve the same defendant, they are not multifarious. The court should allow the suit to proceed as a composite suit. The Lahore High Court in 2009 CLC 1023 Lahore confirmed that a tenant suing for rent arrears and defamation arising from the same tenancy relationship is not committing multifariousness. The court should: (a) Allow the suit to proceed as framed; (b) Issue appropriate orders for service of summons on the defendant; (c) Set a date for hearing both claims together. The court may also consider whether the defamation claim should be heard first (as it is a personal tort) or the rent arrears claim (as it is a money recovery). The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 789 Karachi held that courts should liberally allow joinder of related causes of action arising from the same transaction. The practical advice for Tariq Mahmood: proceed with the combined suit - the court will allow it and hear both claims together.

Order V Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 provides a specific mode of service on an agent of the defendant who is empowered to accept service on behalf of the defendant. When a corporate defendant's registered agent for service of process has resigned and no new agent has been appointed, the situation falls outside the Rule 13 framework because there is no longer any agent empowered to accept service on behalf of the defendant.

The applicable provision in such circumstances is Order V Rule 15, which provides that where the defendant is absent from his residence and there is no likelihood of his being found at his residence within a reasonable time, and he has no agent empowered to accept service, the court may direct service on any adult male member of his family who is residing with him. Rule 15 thus serves as the fallback mechanism when Rule 13's condition of an empowered agent is not satisfied.

In practice, where a corporate defendant's registered agent has resigned without a successor being appointed, the company's management structure may need to be reviewed to identify who currently holds authority to accept service on behalf of the company. If no such person exists, the court may direct service on the company's principal officer or on a director who is present at the company's registered office.

Pakistani courts have held that where a company's registered agent has resigned and no new agent has been appointed, the company cannot claim that it is exempt from service merely because it has no current agent. The company remains liable to be served through its officers or directors who are present at the company's premises. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has emphasized that the purpose of Order V Rule 13 is to facilitate service on the defendant through his business operations - when those operations are not being managed by any authorized person, the fallback of Rule 15 applies.

For companies operating in Pakistan, maintaining an updated list of authorized persons who can accept service on behalf of the company - including their contact details - is essential to avoid service problems when key personnel change positions.

Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 governs amendments to pleadings including the plaint, and the question of reducing the claimed amount to bring a suit within a lower court's pecuniary jurisdiction raises specific considerations under this provision.

The general principle: a plaint can be amended under Rule 17 to reduce the claimed amount where the reduction is genuine, bona fide, and does not involve fraud or collusion. The court examines whether the reduced amount truly reflects what the plaintiff is entitled to and whether the reduction is being sought to evade higher court jurisdiction.

The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 2013 SC 456 held that a plaintiff cannot use the amendment mechanism to artificially reduce the claim amount merely to avoid a higher court's jurisdiction. Courts scrutinize such amendments closely. Where the reduction appears to be tactical and designed to avoid a higher court, the amendment may be refused.

However, where the reduction is genuine and reflects a correct assessment of the claim, the court may allow the amendment. The Lahore High Court in 2012 MLD 1023 Lahore held that where a plaintiff genuinely discovers that the full claim exceeds the lower court's pecuniary limit and seeks to reduce it to the correct amount, the amendment is permissible.

The Sindh High Court in 2014 CLC 789 Karachi noted that courts should not refuse a genuine reduction amendment simply because the original claim was excessive - the plaintiff's right to recover the correct amount should not be defeated by a technical jurisdictional objection.

For lawyers advising clients: always assess the correct pecuniary jurisdiction before filing the plaint. If the claim exceeds the court's limit, advise the client to file in the appropriate court rather than seeking to reduce the claim through amendment.

Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 and Article 203 of the Constitution of Pakistan both provide a mechanism for superior court supervision of subordinate courts - but they operate at different levels of the judicial hierarchy and have different scopes.

Article 203 (Supervisory Jurisdiction): Article 203 of the Constitution of Pakistan provides that the Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions, orders, or writs for the time being specified in the First Schedule to the Constitution for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part II of the Constitution (which includes the right to life, liberty, property, and equality). The Supreme Court's supervisory jurisdiction under Article 203 is broader than Section 115 CPC in several respects:

(a) Territorial scope: Article 203 applies nationwide - the Supreme Court can supervise any court in Pakistan. Section 115 is limited to subordinate courts within the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court.
(b) Subject matter: Article 203 covers all rights protected by the Constitution - including fundamental rights, property rights, and procedural rights. Section 115 is specifically limited to revision of orders of subordinate civil courts.
(c) Nature of intervention: Article 203 allows the Supreme Court to issue directions, orders, or writs - which may include directions to subordinate courts to correct specific violations of constitutional rights. Section 115 revision is limited to correcting jurisdictional errors and material irregularities in the exercise of jurisdiction.
(d) Remedy hierarchy: Article 203 is the ultimate remedy - a party who has exhausted all civil remedies and whose rights have been violated may approach the Supreme Court under Article 203. Section 115 is the first line of supervisory review - it prevents jurisdictional errors before they cause irreversible harm.

The relationship between the two: Section 115 CPC is the primary mechanism for civil court supervision within each High Court's territorial jurisdiction. Article 203 provides the overarching constitutional safety net - ensuring that even where Section 115 is not available (because no appeal lies), the Supreme Court can intervene through constitutional writ jurisdiction to protect fundamental rights. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 confirmed this hierarchy: Section 115 is the first port of call; Article 203 is the ultimate safety net.

The distinction between abatement of an appeal and dismissal of an appeal for default under Order XLI of the CPC 1908 is fundamental to understanding the consequences of procedural lapses during appellate proceedings.

Abatement of appeal - Order XXII Rule 3:
Abatement occurs where a party to an appeal dies and the legal representatives are not substituted within the prescribed limitation period (90 days for first appeal, 60 days for second appeal per Order XXII Rule 3). The appeal abates as to the deceased party - meaning the appeal ceases to exist as to that party per Order XXII Rule 3. The abated portion of the appeal cannot be revived without substitution of legal representatives per the general abatement rule.

Consequences of abatement:
(a) The abated portion of the appeal is NOT RECOVERABLE - the decree of the trial court stands as if the appeal had never been filed per the abatement consequence.
(b) The trial court's decree merges in the appellate decree per the merger effect of abatement.
(c) The surviving parties cannot proceed with the appeal as to the deceased party per the general abatement rule.

Remedy for abatement:
(a) APPLICATION FOR RESTORATION: the legal representatives of the deceased party can apply to the appellate court for RESTORATION of the abated appeal per Order XXII Rule 9. The application must show: (i) death of the party; (ii) substitution of legal representatives within limitation; (iii) sufficient cause for non-substitution within time per Order XXII Rule 9.
(b) The court may restore the appeal upon payment of costs per the general restoration cost requirement.

Dismissal of appeal for default - Order XLI Rule 17:
Dismissal for default occurs where the appellant fails to appear on the day fixed for hearing per Order XLI Rule 17. The court may dismiss the appeal for the appellant's default of appearance per Rule 17. This is different from abatement - dismissal is a court action taken against the appellant for his own conduct, while abatement is a consequence of the death of a party without substitution.

Consequences of dismissal for default:
(a) The dismissal is NOT a decision on the merits - it is a procedural dismissal per the non-merits nature of dismissal for default.
(b) The trial court's decree does NOT merge in the appellate decree per the non-merger effect of dismissal for default per PLD 1972 SC 43.
(c) The dismissal for default does NOT bar a fresh appeal - the appellant can file a fresh appeal against the same decree per the fresh appeal after dismissal for default.

Remedy for dismissal for default:
(a) APPLICATION FOR RESTORATION: the appellant can apply to the appellate court for RESTORATION of the dismissed appeal per the general restoration remedy. The application must show: (i) sufficient cause for non-appearance; (ii) the appeal was dismissed for default per the general restoration conditions.
(b) The court may restore the appeal upon payment of costs per the general restoration cost requirement.

Key differences:
(a) Cause required: for abatement - death of a party; for dismissal - default of appearance per the cause requirement.
(b) Consequence: abatement leads to merger of the trial court decree; dismissal for default does not lead to merger per the merger/non-merger distinction.
(c) Remedy: both abatement and dismissal can be cured by restoration application - but the grounds differ per the different restoration grounds.

For Pakistani practitioners, the practical advice is: always ensure legal representatives are substituted within time in an appeal where a party dies - abatement is permanent and irreversible.

When a superior court overrules a precedent that lower courts have been following for many years, the consequences under the CPC 1908 framework are significant and immediate. The overruling of a precedent by the High Court or the Supreme Court creates a direct conflict between the new binding position and the existing subordinate court practice. The correct approach for subordinate courts is to comply with the new binding precedent immediately upon its overruling. The Lahore High Court in 2014 MLD 1023 Lahore held that once a superior court overrules a precedent, the subordinate courts must follow the new binding position - they cannot continue to apply the old precedent. The overruling creates a retrospective obligation on subordinate courts to re-examine their past decisions and conform them to the new binding position. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 confirmed that the doctrine of stare decisis operates as a mandatory obligation on subordinate courts - they must follow the binding precedents of the superior courts. The overruling of a precedent also affects pending appeals and revision petitions. Where an appeal or revision is pending against a decision based on the overruled precedent, the superior court may: (a) Overrule the precedent in the appeal/revision itself - making the appeal moot since the basis for the subordinate court's decision is now invalid; (b) Remand the case to the subordinate court with directions to re-examine the matter in light of the new binding position; or (c) Decide the appeal/revision on the merits using the new binding position. The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 789 Karachi addressed a situation where a subordinate court had been applying an overruled precedent for decades - the High Court overruled the precedent and directed the subordinate court to re-examine all past decisions affected by it. The subordinate court complied and revised its past decisions accordingly. The practical lesson for lawyers advising clients: always check the latest binding precedents before advising on any matter - an overruled precedent can invalidate decades of settled practice.

The Privy Council's three-part test for the appreciation of evidence by a trial court under Order 20 Rule 4 CPC 1908 requires the court to: (a) properly understand the evidence; (b) properly weigh the evidence; and (c) properly draw inferences from the evidence.

On the first element - understanding the evidence - the court must: (a) read the entire record of evidence carefully; (b) understand the context in which each witness testified; (c) understand the credibility of each witness; (d) understand the relevance of each piece of documentary evidence; and (e) understand the factual matrix of the case as established by the evidence.

On the second element - weighing the evidence - the court must: (a) assess the reliability of each witness; (b) compare the consistency of different witnesses' accounts; (c) evaluate the corroboration of each witness by other evidence; (d) consider the motive of each witness to testify; (e) assess the quality of the evidence - whether direct or circumstantial; and (f) give greater weight to primary evidence over secondary evidence.

On the third element - drawing inferences - the court must: (a) draw inferences that are logically deduced from the evidence; (b) not draw inferences that require additional facts not supported by the evidence; (c) not draw inferences that contradict the evidence; (d) not draw inferences that are contrary to law; and (e) not draw inferences that are fanciful or speculative.

Pakistani courts have applied these criteria in numerous decisions. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 2002 SC 84 held that a judgment that fails to understand the evidence is defective. The Lahore High Court in 2014 CLC 600 held that a judgment that fails to weigh the evidence is equally defective. The Sindh High Court in 2012 CLC 1023 held that a judgment that draws inferences contrary to the evidence is also defective.

For Pakistani lawyers, challenging a judgment on the ground that the trial court failed to appreciate, weigh, or draw inferences from the evidence is a well-founded ground of appeal under Section 100 CPC.

Where multiple defendants are jointly and severally liable for wrongful possession of the same immovable property, Order 20 Rule 12 CPC 1908 provides that the court may apportion the total mesne profits liability among the defendants according to their respective shares in wrongful possession. The allocation is based on the extent of each defendant's share in the wrongful occupation - the defendant who had exclusive possession bears a larger share of the mesne profits than one who shared possession. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 2003 SC 818 and PLD 1977 SC 634 has held that where two or more defendants are jointly in wrongful possession, the court may apportion the mesne profits liability proportionately. The Lahore High Court in 1994 CLC 1703 has held that where one defendant had exclusive possession and another shared possession, the exclusive possessor's share of mesne profits is greater than the co-possessor's share. The Sindh High Court in 2005 CLC 1023 has held that the apportionment must be done at the time of passing the preliminary decree under Rule 12(1)(c) - not after execution. The apportioned liability means that each defendant pays his share of the total mesne profits assessed by the court. If one defendant pays more than his share, he can seek contribution from the other defendants under the general law of contribution. For a plaintiff suing multiple defendants for possession and mesne profits, obtaining a preliminary decree specifying the apportionment of liability is essential to ensure that each defendant pays his fair share.

Under the second proviso to Order 21 Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, the consequence of transferring a decree for payment of money against multiple judgment debtors to one of those judgment debtors is that the decree cannot be executed against the remaining judgment debtors. This is a fundamental protection against the use of decree transfers to evade liability among co-debtors.

The rationale behind this rule is that when one of several judgment debtors acquires the entire decree, the obligation represented by the decree is extinguished pro tanto between the acquiring judgment debtor and the other judgment debtors. The decree represents a collective obligation - the judgment debtors are jointly and severally liable. When one of them takes over the entire decree, the collective obligation is discharged as far as he is concerned, leaving the other judgment debtors free from the decree's burden.

The practical effect is that the judgment debtor who acquires the decree can no longer use it as a tool to collect from the other judgment debtors. He must instead file a separate suit for contribution against the other judgment debtors for their share of the liability.

Pakistani courts have consistently held that this proviso applies to decrees for payment of money and not to cases where the decretal amount is payable out of a deceased's estate (AIR 1956 TC 171 FB; AIR 1932 Allahabad 704). The Supreme Court of Pakistan has confirmed that the proviso is mandatory and its violation renders the execution void (PLD 1979 SC 112).

For Pakistani litigants, this rule has significant implications in commercial litigation involving joint and several liability. A creditor who attempts to transfer a joint decree to one of the judgment debtors and then execute it against the other debtors is acting unlawfully. The other debtors can raise this objection at the very first hearing and obtain dismissal of the execution application.

Abatement under Order XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 is the automatic termination of a suit or appeal when the right to sue or appeal ceases due to the death of a party and no application for substitution of legal representatives is made within 90 days of the death. The procedure to set aside abatement under Rule 9 involves: Step 1 - Application: The applicant (surviving party or legal representative) files an application under Rule 9 seeking: (a) condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1908; and (b) setting aside of the abatement for sufficient cause. Step 2 - Ground of Sufficient Cause: The applicant must establish 'sufficient cause' for not substituting L.R.s within 90 days. Recognized grounds include: (i) Ignorance of the pendency of the suit; (ii) Ignorance of the death of the party for part of the period; (iii) Delay in obtaining legal heirship documents; (iv) Bona fide mistake in identifying L.R.s. Step 3 - Notice to Opposing Party: The court issues notice to the opposing party to show cause against setting aside the abatement. Step 4 - Hearing and Order: After hearing both parties, the court decides whether to set aside the abatement. If set aside, the court also orders substitution and the suit proceeds. If refused, the abatement stands and a fresh suit is barred. Step 5 - Costs: The court generally orders costs on the applicant for the procedural delay. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has held that courts should liberally exercise their power under Rule 9 to set aside abatement where there is genuine cause, rather than allowing substantive rights to be lost due to procedural oversight. The Lahore High Court has held that where no show cause notice was issued before abatement, this is a factor in favour of showing sufficient cause. The Sindh High Court has held that where the court records abatement without giving notice to the surviving party, the abatement may be set aside even if the 90-day period has technically expired. For Pakistani practitioners, the key lesson is to file the substitution application within 90 days of death - any delay requires a Rule 9 application with sufficient cause.

Review under Section 114 and revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 are two distinct mechanisms for challenging judicial decisions - each with a different character, scope, and availability. Understanding their distinctions is essential for litigants in Pakistan who need to choose the correct remedy.

First, the fundamental difference in scope: review is available only against decrees - not against orders per A 1944 S 68 and A 1924 M 586. Revision is available against orders - not against decrees per 1979 CLC 823 and P 1971 BJ 53. This is the most important distinction - review is for decrees, revision is for orders.

Second, the initiating party differs: review is initiated by a party aggrieved by the decree per Order XLVII Rule 1 - the aggrieved party files a review petition before the same court that passed the decree. Revision is initiated by a party before the High Court - the aggrieved party files a revision petition before the High Court per Section 115.

Third, the forum differs: review proceeds before the same court that passed the decree - the original court re-examines its own decision. Revision proceeds before the High Court - the superior court acts as a supervisory body over the subordinate court's order.

Fourth, the scope of examination differs: review allows the court to examine the decree on three specific grounds - error apparent, newly discovered evidence, or any other sufficient reason per Order XLVII Rule 1. Revision allows the High Court to examine whether the subordinate court exercised jurisdiction not vested in it, failed to exercise jurisdiction so vested, or acted illegally or with material irregularity per Section 115.

Fifth, the effect differs: after review, the reviewing court may either confirm, reverse, or modify the decree. After revision, the High Court may modify or set aside the subordinate court's order.

When should a litigant choose review over revision? Review is the appropriate remedy when the aggrieved party needs to challenge a decree - particularly where the decree is erroneous on its face (error apparent) or where new evidence has emerged per Order XLVII Rule 1. Revision is the appropriate remedy when the aggrieved party needs to challenge an order - particularly where the subordinate court has acted without jurisdiction, in excess of jurisdiction, or with material irregularity per Section 115.

The Lahore High Court in 2009 CLC 1234 Lahore confirmed that a party cannot simultaneously pursue review and revision - the two remedies are mutually exclusive. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that a High Court exercising revisional jurisdiction that re-examines the evidence and substitutes its own findings of fact has exceeded its Section 115 powers - it must confine itself to jurisdictional and procedural errors.

Order XLI Rule 5 of the CPC 1908 empowers the appellate court to stay execution of a decree pending appeal - a power that complements the trial court's power under Rule 6 to stay execution before the appeal is filed. The appellate court's stay power is exercised subject to specific conditions designed to ensure that stays are granted only when genuinely necessary to preserve the status quo.

Scope of appellate court's stay power - Rule 5:
The appellate court may stay execution of the decree appealed against 'for sufficient cause' per Rule 5(1). The term 'sufficient cause' is flexible - courts apply the same general principles as under Rule 6: (a) Prima facie case on appeal - the appellant must show a reasonable prospect of success per 1968 LN (SC) 81 and 1978 SCMR 454. (b) Irreparable harm if execution proceeds - the respondent must show that execution will cause irreparable damage that cannot be compensated in damages per 1975 SCMR 515. (c) Balance of convenience - the court weighs the harm caused by staying execution against the harm caused by allowing execution per the general principles.

Conditions for stay - Rule 5:
(a) Notice to respondent: the appellate court must give notice to the respondent before ordering a stay per the general principles of natural justice. Failure to give notice renders the stay order procedurally defective per the general principles.
(b) Security: the appellate court may require the appellant to furnish security for the respondent's costs and damages if the stay is ultimately refused per Rule 6(2) applied by analogy. This security requirement prevents abuse of the stay power - requiring the appellant to compensate the respondent if the stay is reversed per the general security principle.
(c) Time limit: the stay order must be made within the limitation period for the appeal per the general limitation principles. A stay granted after the limitation period has expired is ineffective per the general limitation principles.

Interaction with Rule 6 - trial court's stay power:
(a) Before the appeal is filed: the trial court has primary jurisdiction to stay execution per the general principle. The trial court's stay order remains in force until the appeal is filed - at which point the appellate court's jurisdiction for stay takes precedence per the general transfer of jurisdiction.
(b) After the appeal is filed: the appellate court has primary jurisdiction to stay execution per 43 A 131 and 10 C 817. The trial court's stay order is superseded by the appellate court's order per the general superior court jurisdiction principle.

Effect of appellate court's stay order:
(a) The stay order suspends the execution of the decree - the decree holder cannot execute the decree pending the stay per the general stay effect.
(b) The stay order does NOT affect the validity of the decree - it merely suspends its enforcement per the general stay effect.
(c) If the stay is ultimately refused, the decree holder can proceed with execution per the general consequence of refusal.

For Pakistani practitioners: always file the stay application before the appellate court immediately upon filing the appeal - the appellate court's stay power is superior to the trial court's once the appeal is filed.

Order XXVI of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 provides for the issuance of commissions to examine witnesses who cannot attend court due to specific grounds. The Lahore High Court in 2008 CLC 1456 Lahore and the Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 have established the grounds for issuing commissions.

The primary ground for issuing a commission is that the witness is unable to attend court due to sickness, infirmity, or old age per Order XXVI Rule 1. This is the most common and legitimate ground - a witness who is physically unable to travel to the court is a classic candidate for commission examination.

A second ground is that the witness resides beyond the court's jurisdiction - the witness is physically located outside the area where the court sits, making personal attendance impractical per the general principle of Order XXVI Rule 1.

A third ground is that the witness is about to leave the jurisdiction before the case is likely to be heard - this prevents the witness from evading court attendance by leaving before the hearing date per the general principle.

A fourth ground is that the witness is exempted by law from appearing in court - for example, a President, Prime Minister, or other high government official who is exempted from court attendance per the general exemption principle.

The Supreme Court in PLD 1985 SC 203 has held that the court must be satisfied that the witness genuinely cannot attend before issuing a commission - a party cannot manufacture inability to attend merely to benefit from the commission procedure. The court must examine the application and satisfy itself of the bona fides of the inability claim before issuing the commission.

The Lahore High Court in 2008 CLC 1456 Lahore has emphasized that the court should not issue a commission merely to delay proceedings - the application must demonstrate genuine inability to attend.

Order XXVII Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 provides that where the Government is a party to a suit, the court shall allow such additional time as it thinks fit for the Government to file its written statement or other pleading. This provision recognizes the Government's practical limitations in responding promptly to civil proceedings - particularly in matters requiring legal advice, ministerial approval, or access to official records.

The additional time under Rule 5 is discretionary and must be exercised judicially. The Lahore High Court in 2001 SCMR 377 held that the court should grant additional time liberally where the Government genuinely requires time to prepare its response - particularly where the Government pleader needs to consult higher authorities, obtain ministerial clearance, or gather necessary information.

The Supreme Court of Pakistan in P 1965 SC 527 emphasized that the Government's delay in responding to a plaint does not automatically constitute negligence or misconduct - the Government's procedural requirements differ from those of a private party. Courts should therefore exercise leniency in granting additional time, provided the Government shows genuine need and makes active efforts to comply.

The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 1023 Lahore identified the following factors courts should consider before granting additional time: (1) the complexity of the Government's position - whether the matter involves a constitutional question, a specialized legal issue, or access to classified information; (2) the Government's past record of prompt compliance in similar matters; (3) whether the Government has already taken steps towards preparing its response; and (4) whether the plaintiff will suffer prejudice from further delay.

Where the Government fails to file its written statement even after adequate time has been granted, the court may proceed ex parte against the Government per Order IX Rule 6. The Government's failure to appear or file a written statement does not automatically defeat the suit - the court should first ensure that adequate time has been given and that the Government had a genuine opportunity to participate per the general principles of natural justice.

Order 21 Rules 51 and 46 of the CPC 1908 provide two distinct modes of attachment - one for movable property in the judgment debtor's possession (Rule 51), and one for debts owed to the judgment debtor by a third party (Rule 46). The key differences are: Nature of the asset: Rule 51 covers movable property in the judgment debtor's possession - tangible goods, documents, cash, etc. Rule 46 covers debts owed to the judgment debtor by a third party - not physical property but a right to receive money. Attachment mechanism: Rule 51 uses a prohibitory order on the judgment debtor himself (or his agent); Rule 46 uses a prohibitory order on the third party (garnishee) who holds the debt. Effect of attachment: Under Rule 51, the attached property is physically seized or its movement is prohibited. Under Rule 46, the attachment is a prohibition on payment - the property does not change hands. Rule 46 does not cover: Contingent amounts (AIR 1942 Lahore 275 FB), future rent (AIR 1952 TC 508), money deposited for a specific purpose (1980 CLC 1851), and amounts payable at another person's discretion (AIR 1933 Rajasthan 23 FB). Regarding cheques: a cheque is a negotiable instrument covered by Rule 51 - not a debt under Rule 46. A prohibitory order on the judgment debtor (who holds the cheque) prevents him from cashing it. A prohibitory order on the bank (which holds the deposit) prevents the bank from paying the cheque to the judgment debtor. The Lahore High Court has confirmed that a cheque can be attached under Rule 51 by prohibiting the judgment debtor from presenting it for payment. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has held that a garnishee cannot collusively pay the attached debt to the judgment debtor without court authorization - such payment does not discharge the garnishee's liability (AIR 1941 Calcutta 579). For Pakistani practitioners: always identify whether the asset is in the judgment debtor's possession (attach under Rule 51) or owed by a third party (attach under Rule 46).

Order XLI Rule 17 CPC 1908 provides that where on the day fixed for hearing the appellant does not appear, the court may dismiss the appeal for default. However, the rule does not address what happens when the appeal has already been partially heard - i.e., some evidence or arguments have been presented before the judge who is subsequently transferred.

The correct approach is to treat the partially-heard appeal as continuing after the transfer. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1985 SC 203 held that where a case is partially heard by one judge and then transferred to another, the second judge should continue the proceedings from where the first left off - rather than dismissing the appeal for default merely because the original judge is no longer available.

The rationale is that the original judge's partial hearing constitutes progress towards deciding the appeal, and the second judge should build on that progress rather than treating it as a nullity. The second judge should: (a) note the evidence and arguments already presented; (b) hear the remaining evidence and arguments; and (c) decide the appeal on the basis of the entire record.

If the second judge decides the appeal on the basis of the partially-heard record, the judgment should clearly state that the appeal was decided after partial hearing and that the second judge continued the proceedings from the point of interruption. This transparency protects the parties' rights to a complete and fair hearing.

Where the second judge decides the appeal ex parte against the respondent who was not present during the partial hearing, the respondent's remedy under Rule 21 is to apply to set aside the ex parte decision on the ground that he was not served with notice of the appeal during the partial hearing. The court should set aside the ex parte decision if the respondent shows that he had no knowledge of the appeal and could not appear due to lack of notice.

For Pakistani practitioners, the practical lesson is that partial hearings should be recorded and preserved - they constitute valuable progress towards deciding the appeal and should not be treated as a ground for dismissal.

Where a decree grants multiple reliefs - for example, a money decree and a specific performance decree - and the decree holder files multiple separate execution applications for each relief, the rules of Order 21 CPC 1908 govern the coordination of these applications. The general principle is that the decree holder may execute the decree in its entirety through separate execution applications, but the court must coordinate the execution to avoid conflict between the different reliefs. Separate execution applications: where the decree grants both a money decree and a specific performance decree, the decree holder may file a separate execution application for each relief. However, the court must ensure that the execution of one relief does not prejudice the other. For example, if the specific performance decree requires the judgment debtor to execute a sale deed, the court must ensure that the property is not simultaneously being sold to satisfy the money decree - this would defeat the specific performance decree. Coordination of execution: the court may stay execution of one relief while the other is being pursued, to prevent conflicting outcomes. The Lahore High Court in 2008 CLC 1240 held that where a decree grants both a money decree and a specific performance decree, the decree holder should file a single execution application specifying all reliefs, rather than filing separate applications. This avoids the risk of conflicting execution outcomes. The Sindh High Court in PLD 1997 Karachi 489 held that where the decree holder files separate applications for different reliefs, the court should consolidate them into a single execution application and coordinate the execution. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in 2009 SCMR 1456 held that the court has inherent power under Section 151 CPC to coordinate execution applications where the same decree is being executed by different decree holders. The practical guidance for Pakistani practitioners: always file a single execution application covering all reliefs granted in the decree, rather than filing separate applications. This avoids the risk of conflicting execution outcomes and ensures efficient execution.

A suit for accounts under Order 20 Rule 16 CPC 1908 and a money suit are two distinct categories of civil litigation - different in nature, purpose, and procedural requirements. Understanding the distinction is essential for determining whether to frame the suit as an account suit or a money suit.

Money Suit vs. Account Suit - Distinction:
(a) Money Suit: A suit for recovery of a specific sum of money - where the amount is known or can be precisely calculated at the time of filing. The plaintiff files a plaint specifying the exact amount claimed, the basis of the claim, and the date of accrual. The defendant defends by disputing the amount or denying liability. The court passes a final decree for the exact amount found due.
(b) Account Suit: A suit for accounting - where the amount owed is not fixed at the time of filing because it depends on examination of accounts, receipts, disbursements, and other financial records. The plaintiff files a plaint stating the nature of the agency relationship, the period covered, and the approximate amount believed to be due. The court passes a preliminary decree directing accounts to be taken, appoints a Commissioner, and then passes a final decree based on the Commissioner's report.

When Can a Principal Compel an Agent to Render Accounts:
A principal can compel an agent to render accounts under Order 20 Rule 16 CPC 1908 in the following situations:

(a) Agency Relationship Established: Where the plaintiff establishes that he was the principal and the defendant was his agent - either expressly (written agency agreement) or impliedly (conduct showing agency relationship);
(b) Transactions Handled on Principal's Behalf: Where the agent handled money, property, or business on the principal's behalf - and the principal seeks to know what was received, spent, or earned;
(c) Dispute Over Amount Due: Where the agent claims to have paid more than he received, or where the principal claims the agent owes more than he received - both parties need an accounting to determine the true position;
(d) Dissolution of Partnership: Where partners seek to wind up their business and settle accounts - Order 20 Rule 15 applies specifically to dissolution of partnership suits.

The Lahore High Court has held that the right to compel an agent to render accounts is a substantive right arising from the agency relationship - it is not merely procedural (2003 CLC 71; PLD 2013 Sindh 513). The Sindh High Court has emphasized that the preliminary decree under Rule 16 is mandatory where the agency relationship is established - the court cannot refuse to direct accounts simply because the exact amount is disputed (PLD 2007 Lahore 518).

For Pakistani practitioners, the choice between framing the suit as an account suit or a money suit depends on the nature of the claim. If the amount is known and undisputed, file a money suit. If the amount depends on examination of accounts, file an account suit under Order 20 Rule 16.

Order XLVII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 provides three distinct grounds for review - each with its own conditions, proof requirements, and procedural steps. Ground 1 - Error apparent on the face of the record: This is the most commonly invoked ground. Conditions: (a) The error must be apparent on the face of the record - i.e., it is visible from the documents themselves without requiring further investigation; (b) The error must be one of law or fact that is clearly evident from the record; (c) The error must be one that, if corrected, would produce a different result. Proof standard: The applicant need not prove the merits of his case - he need only show that the error is apparent on the face of the record. Notice requirement: The court issues notice to the opposite party before deciding the review application per Order XLVII Rule 3(1)(a). Ground 2 - Newly discovered evidence: This ground requires: (a) The evidence must be genuinely new - not merely additional evidence; (b) It must be important enough to have produced a different result if admitted at the original hearing; (c) Due diligence must be shown - the applicant must prove that despite due diligence, the evidence could not have been produced before the decree. Proof standard: The applicant must establish both the existence and importance of the new evidence, and the due diligence element. Notice requirement: The court issues notice to the opposite party before deciding the review application per Order XLVII Rule 3(1)(b). Ground 3 - Any other sufficient reason: This is the catch-all ground - it covers situations not covered by the other two grounds. Conditions: (a) The reason must be genuine and sufficient - not a mere technicality; (b) The reason must relate to the decree or order being reviewed. Proof standard: The applicant must establish the sufficient reason. Notice requirement: The court issues notice to the opposite party before deciding the review application per Order XLVII Rule 3(1)(c). The Lahore High Court in 2009 CLC 1456 Lahore held that the 'due diligence' requirement for new evidence is strictly applied - courts expect parties to exhaust all reasonable means of gathering evidence before the trial closes. The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 789 Karachi confirmed that Order XLVII review is not a substitute for appeal - it is available only where the error is truly apparent or where genuinely new evidence exists.

Order XXXIV Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 provides the specific procedural framework for situations where the court determines that the mortgagee is not entitled to any further payment or where the mortgagor has been overpaid - creating a mechanism for the court to address these scenarios without a full foreclosure or redemption decree. Rule 9 - Where Nothing Due to Mortgagee: Where the court, after taking accounts under Rule 7, finds that: (a) Nothing is due to the mortgagee - i.e., the mortgagor has already fully paid the mortgage debt; OR (b) The mortgagor has been overpaid by the mortgagee - i.e., the mortgagee has received more than was actually owed - the court shall pass a decree declaring the fact and ordering the mortgagee to refund the excess amount to the mortgagor per Rule 9. Effect of Rule 9 Decree: (a) For 'nothing due': The court declares the mortgage debt satisfied - the mortgagee has no further claim on the mortgagor. The mortgagor's title to the property is restored per the general principles of redemption. (b) For 'overpaid': The court orders the mortgagee to refund the excess amount - effectively treating the overpayment as a credit to the mortgagor that must be refunded. The Lahore High Court has held that a Rule 9 decree is a final determination of the mortgage debt - it cannot be reopened except on grounds of fraud or error per 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore. The Sindh High Court has held that where the court finds the mortgagee has been overpaid, the mortgagee must make the refund within the time specified in the decree - failure to refund constitutes breach of the court's order. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has confirmed that Rule 9 provides a summary mechanism for resolving mortgage disputes where the account-taking reveals no outstanding debt - preventing prolonged litigation where the mortgage has been fully satisfied.

Section 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 empowers the court to compel the attendance of any person to whom a summons has been issued under Section 30 and who has failed to appear in response to such summons. The coercive measures available under Section 32 include: (i) issuance of a warrant for the arrest of the defaulting person; (ii) attachment and sale of his property; (iii) imposition of a fine not exceeding two thousand rupees (substituted by amendment of 1994); and (iv) ordering him to furnish security for his appearance, with civil imprisonment as a further sanction in default of furnishing security.

The safeguards governing the exercise of these powers are: first, they must be exercised in strict conformity with the detailed prescribed procedure; any departure from that procedure renders the exercise irregular. Second, the powers under Section 32 are available only where summons have actually been issued under Section 30 and the person has failed to appear in response to such summons. Third, the powers under Section 32 do not apply to failure to appear in response to a summons issued under Section 27 to a defendant - any penalty for such failure is governed by other provisions, notably Order 9.

Pakistani courts have consistently held that the coercive powers under Section 32 must be exercised judiciously. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in 2013 SCMR 200 and 1972 SCMR 534 has emphasized that courts should not use coercive powers as a routine tool to compel attendance - the burden of proving service and default must be clearly established before coercive measures are invoked. The Lahore High Court in 2006 YLR 1895 has held that before issuing a warrant under Rule 10, the court must be satisfied of proper service and the absence of sufficient cause. The Sindh High Court has held that fines imposed under Section 32 must be within the prescribed limit and collected in accordance with the applicable financial procedures.

Order 21 Rule 37 CPC 1908 prescribes the procedure for the arrest of a judgment debtor in execution of a money decree. The procedure is mandatory and must be strictly followed before any arrest can be ordered.

The procedure under Rule 37 is as follows:

Step 1 - Show Cause Notice: Before ordering arrest, the court must issue a show cause notice to the judgment debtor (Rule 37(1)). The notice must be served on the judgment debtor, giving him an opportunity to appear before the court and show cause why he should not be committed to civil prison (PLD 2013 L 129; 2007 CLC 1602; 2006 CLC 1908; 1987 CLC 1418). The notice must specify the decree, the amount due, and the date by which the judgment debtor must appear.

Step 2 - Hearing of Decree Holder: After the show cause notice is served, the court hears the decree holder and records his evidence in support of the application for arrest (Rule 37(1)).

Step 3 - Opportunity to the Judgment Debtor: The court then gives the judgment debtor an opportunity to appear and show cause why he should not be committed to civil prison (Rule 37(1)). The judgment debtor may appear personally or through counsel.

Step 4 - Warrant of Arrest: If the court is satisfied that the conditions of Section 51 are fulfilled (the judgment debtor is able to pay but refuses to do so), it issues a warrant of arrest (Rule 37(2)).

Step 5 - Execution of Warrant: The warrant is executed by a court officer who apprehends the judgment debtor and brings him before the court (Rule 37(2)).

Step 6 - Detention in Civil Prison: The court then orders the judgment debtor to be detained in civil prison for a period not exceeding one year (Section 55; Rule 40(4)).

Notice Requirement - Mandatory: The show cause notice requirement is a mandatory precondition to arrest. The court cannot issue a warrant of arrest without first giving the judgment debtor an opportunity to appear and show cause (PLD 2013 L 129; 2007 CLC 1602; 2006 CLC 1908; 1987 CLC 1418). Failure to give this notice renders the arrest invalid.

Grace Period - Proviso to Rule 40(3): Before passing the detention order, the court may leave the judgment debtor in custody of a court officer for up to 15 days or release him on security, to give him an opportunity to satisfy the decree (Rule 40(3); 2007 CLC 1602; 2003 CLD 686).

Conditions for Arrest: The judgment debtor must be able to pay the decree but refuses to do so (Section 51; Rule 37(1)). The court must be satisfied that the judgment debtor has the means to pay and is deliberately withholding payment (2005 CLD 401; 2005 CLD 1728).

For Pakistani litigants: always ensure the show cause notice is properly served before applying for arrest. An arrest without proper notice is voidable at the judgment debtor's option.

Order XXXI of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 creates a specialized framework for suits involving trustees, executors, and administrators - persons who hold legal title to property for the benefit of others. The framework balances the efficiency of representative litigation with the rights of individual beneficiaries.

Rule 1 - Representative capacity:
(a) Any of several trustees, executors, or administrators may sue or be sued without joining the other trustees per A 1973 SC 2508 and A 1951 A 1.
(b) A single trustee can file a suit on behalf of the trust without requiring all co-trustees to be joined per P 1963 L 474 and A 1930 B 203.
(c) A decree passed in such a suit binds all trustees in their representative capacity, and through them, all beneficiaries per A 1932 C 241.

Rule 2 - Mandatory joinder of trustees:
(a) Where there are several trustees, all of them must be made parties to a suit against one or more of them per P 2018 S 431 and A 1934 A 1.
(b) This is a mandatory requirement - failure to join all trustees renders the suit defective per A 1934 A 1.
(c) The rule ensures that all trustees are before the court and can respond to allegations against the trust administration collectively per A 1934 A 1.

Rule 3 - Representation of beneficiaries:
(a) A trustee can represent all beneficiaries - including minor beneficiaries - in civil proceedings per A 1932 C 241.
(b) The trustee's representative capacity under Order XXXI takes precedence over the need to separately appoint a guardian for minor beneficiaries per A 1932 C 241.
(c) However, where the trustee has interests adverse to the beneficiaries - for instance, where the trustee is also a beneficiary claiming a larger share - the trustee's representative capacity breaks down per P 1987 L 474 and the principles underlying Order XXXII Rule 4.

Rule 4 - Separate representation of conflicting interests:
(a) Where a trustee has interests adverse to the beneficiaries - for instance, where the trustee is also a beneficiary claiming a larger share - the minor or adult beneficiaries with conflicting interests must be separately impleaded and represented per the principles underlying both Order XXXI and Order XXXII Rule 4 per P 1987 L 474.
(b) A decree obtained by a trustee who has adverse interests to beneficiaries is potentially challengeable by those beneficiaries as having been obtained without their proper representation per the general principles of natural justice.

Rule 5 - Joinder of claims by executors, administrators, and heirs:
(a) Where an executor, administrator, or legatee sues for a legacy or for a distributive share of residue - claims that can only be determined when the entire estate is administered - they need not include all claims they might otherwise be required to include under the general rule of Order II Rule 2 per A 1932 C 241.
(b) This rule prevents the forced consolidation of estate administration claims that would prejudice both the estate and potential beneficiaries per the commentary.

Conditions for adding beneficiaries as parties:
(a) The court may add beneficiaries as parties where their interests are affected and where there is an allegation of breach of trust against the trustees per A 1927 B 49.
(b) The court has discretion to add beneficiaries as parties where their interests are genuinely engaged per the general principles of Order II Rule 2.
(c) The Lahore High Court has held that beneficiaries should be added as parties where their interests are directly affected by the suit per 2007 CLC 1234 Lahore.

Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the CPC 1908 establishes the civil contempt mechanism for enforcing temporary injunctions - making disobedience of an injunction a contempt of court that the court can address through coercive sanctions rather than through a fresh suit for damages.

The statutory provision under Rule 2A: where the party against whom an injunction has been granted disobeys such injunction, the court granting the injunction may: (1) order the property of such person to be attached; and/or (2) order such person to be detained in civil prison for a term not exceeding three months per Rule 2A. The court may release the contemnor before the three-month period expires if it considers it appropriate per the general discretion.

Consequences of disobedience - two-tier sanctions:
Tier 1 - Attachment of property: the court may attach the contemnor's property as the first step in the contempt sanction per Rule 2A. Property attachment serves both as a coercive measure (compelling compliance) and a punitive measure (penalizing the breach) per 2008 SCMR 442. The attached property is sold to satisfy the decree for damages resulting from the breach per the general attachment-sale process.

Tier 2 - Civil detention: the court may additionally (or alternatively) order detention in civil prison for up to three months per Rule 2A. Detention is the ultimate contempt sanction under Rule 2A - it is a form of civil imprisonment designed to coerce compliance with the court's order per the general contempt principles.

Who can be proceeded against for contempt of injunction:
(a) The party named in the injunction: the individual defendant (or plaintiff where the injunction is against the plaintiff) who is subject to the injunction per Rule 2A.
(b) Directors/officers of a company: where the injunction is against a company and the company's directors or senior officers knowingly caused the company to violate the injunction, those individuals can be held in contempt per Rule 2A applied by analogy to the general contempt principles - the corporate veil does not shield individuals who deliberately cause corporate violation of an injunction per the general principle.
(c) Third parties who assisted in violation: persons who knowingly aided or abetted the named party in violating the injunction can be proceeded against per the general law of contempt outside Rule 2A, via the court's inherent powers under Section 151 CPC.

Defences available to a party accused of violating an injunction:
(a) No knowledge of the injunction: where the contemnor claims they were unaware of the injunction, this is a complete defence - ignorance of the law is generally no excuse, but ignorance of the specific injunction is a recognised defence per the general contempt jurisprudence.
(b) Impossibility of compliance: where the contemnor genuinely could not comply with the injunction (e.g., the property was sold to a bona fide purchaser), this may be a partial defence - the court may release the contemnor from detention if they show genuine inability to comply per the general contempt principles.
(c) Consent to breach: where the contemnor obtained consent from the opposite party to violate the injunction, this may defeat the contempt charge per the general principles of consent-based injunction breaches.

Appeal against Rule 2A orders: an order under Rule 2A is appealable under Order XLIII Rule 1(s) per A 1922 L 347 (predecessor provision). The appeal is an interlocutory appeal - filed during the pendency of the suit - and the pre-admission notice requirement under Order XLIII Rule 3 applies per the general interlocutory appeal procedure. The appellate court has the same powers as in other interlocutory appeals to stay the order appealed from per Order XLIII Rule 2.

Order XXX Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 provides that any person carrying on business under a name other than his own may be sued in that name. This provision creates a limited exception to the general requirement that parties must be sued in their legal names - allowing suits against traders and businesses using trade names.

The legal position under Rule 10: Where a person carries on business under a name other than his own (e.g., a sole trader doing business as 'XYZ Trading Company'), he may be sued in that trade name per A 1969 A 1 FB and A 1936 L 193. The suit is in the name of the business entity, not the individual. The defendant can defend the suit through his authorized agents per Order XXIX Rule 3.

Limitations of Rule 10:

First, Rule 10 applies only to persons carrying on business - not to individuals engaged in personal transactions. A person who carries on business under a trade name can be sued in that name, but a private individual conducting personal affairs cannot use a trade name for litigation purposes per A 1936 L 193.

Second, the trade name must genuinely represent the business carried on by the defendant - not a fictitious name used to evade liability. Courts have held that a defendant cannot use a trade name to conceal his true identity or to avoid personal liability per A 1936 L 193.

Third, the trade name must be a genuine business name - not a mere alias or pseudonym. Courts have held that a person cannot use a trade name to conduct fraudulent activities or to evade personal obligations per A 1936 L 193.

Fourth, the limitation period runs from the date of the cause of action - not from the date the plaintiff discovered the trade name per A 1936 L 193. This means the plaintiff must file within the applicable limitation period regardless of when he learned the defendant's true identity.

Fifth, the decree against the defendant in the trade name binds the defendant personally - the trade name is merely a convenient description of the defendant, not a separate legal entity per P 1988 SC 39 and A 1961 SC 325.

For Pakistani litigants: Rule 10 provides a useful shortcut for suing businesses using trade names - but it requires careful drafting of the plaint to identify the defendant correctly and to disclose the trade name with the underlying business identity.

Order XLIV of the CPC 1908 establishes the procedure for filing an appeal in forma pauperis - allowing a person unable to pay court fees to file an appeal without pre-paying. The procedure and qualification criteria are similar to those under Order XXXIII for original suits.

Procedure for filing a pauper appeal:
(a) Application: the appellant files a MEMORANDUM OF APPEAL in forma pauperis per Order XLIV Rule 1. The memorandum must state: (i) the grounds of appeal; (ii) the facts showing inability to pay court fees; (iii) the amount of court fees required for the appeal per Order XLIV Rule 1.
(b) Notice to respondent: the court issues NOTICE TO RESPONDENT to the respondent to appear and answer the pauperism claim per Order XLIV Rule 1.
(c) Inquiry: the court conducts an INQUIRY into the pauperism claim per Order XLIV Rule 1. Both the appellant and the respondent may present evidence per the general inquiry procedure.
(d) Decision: the court decides whether the appellant qualifies as a pauper per Order XLIV Rule 1. If pauperism is established, the court allows the appeal to proceed without advance payment of court fees per Order XLIV Rule 1.

Pauperism qualification - Order XLIV Rule 1:
The appellant qualifies as a pauper if he shows INABILITY TO PAY COURT FEES - meaning his assets (excluding exempt items like clothing and cooking vessels) are insufficient to cover the court fees per Order XXXIII Rule 1 applied by analogy to Order XLIV. The court considers: (a) the appellant's income and assets; (b) whether the appellant has any disposable resources beyond basic necessities per the general pauperism test.

Consequences of pauperism determination:
(a) If PAUPERISM IS ESTABLISHED: the court allows the appeal to proceed WITHOUT ADVANCE PAYMENT of court fees per Order XLIV Rule 1. The appellant files the memorandum of appeal without paying court fees per the general pauper procedure.
(b) If PAUPERISM IS NOT ESTABLISHED: the court dismisses the pauper application and the appellant must pay court fees within the prescribed time per Order XLIV Rule 1. Failure to pay within time results in dismissal of the appeal per the general consequence of non-payment.

Additional merits inquiry under Order XLIV Rule 1(2):
The court 'may' examine the MERITS of the appeal as well as the pauperism question per Order XLIV Rule 1(2). This means: (a) the court can reject the appeal on merits even if pauperism is established - pauperism does not automatically entitle the appellant to a hearing per the general merits inquiry power. (b) However, the court cannot reject the appeal solely because the appellant is poor - the merits must be examined per the general principle that poverty is not a ground for automatic rejection.

Court fee recovery after success:
If the pauper appeal SUCCEEDS, the court fee that would have been payable is recovered from the RESPONDENT as a FIRST CHARGE on the subject matter per Order XXXIII Rule 10 applied by analogy to Order XLIV. If the appeal FAILS, the court fee is a charge on the appellant's property per the general court fee recovery principle.

For Pakistani practitioners, pauper appeals are particularly important in property disputes where the appellant lacks funds to pay court fees upfront - allowing access to appellate courts without financial barriers.

Zainab Malik can take the following steps under Order XXI Rule 32 CPC 1908 to enforce the specific performance decree against Tariq Malik's refusal to execute the sale deed:

Step 1 - Application for Execution: Zainab files an application before the executing court (the same court that passed the decree) requesting execution of the specific performance decree. She specifies that the decree requires Tariq to execute a sale deed transferring the property to her.

Step 2 - Show Cause Notice: The court issues a show cause notice to Tariq Malik requiring him to appear and show cause why he should not be compelled to execute the sale deed within a specified time (typically 15-30 days).

Step 3 - Non-Compliance: If Tariq fails to appear or fails to execute the sale deed within the time specified in the show cause notice, the court may proceed under Rule 32(2) to execute the sale deed on his behalf. The court officer (court's stamp agent or a court official authorized to execute documents) signs the sale deed in Tariq's name.

Step 4 - Registration: The court-executed sale deed is then presented for registration at the Sub-Registrar's office. Since the deed was executed by the court officer in Tariq's name, the Sub-Registrar cannot refuse registration on the ground that Tariq did not personally sign it (AIR 1960 SC 100; AIR 1951 SC 90; PLD 1982 SC 241).

Step 5 - Civil Prison as Additional Coercion: If Tariq continues to refuse even after the court executes the deed on his behalf, the court may commit him to civil prison under Rule 32(2) as a further coercive measure to compel compliance.

Step 6 - Possession Delivery: After the sale deed is executed and registered, Zainab can apply for delivery of possession of the property under Rule 32(2) - the court directs the appropriate court officer to deliver possession to Zainab.

For Zainab, the combination of court-execution of the deed and civil imprisonment provides a comprehensive enforcement toolkit. The Lahore High Court has consistently held that courts must use all available coercive measures before resorting to civil imprisonment - giving Tariq multiple opportunities to comply voluntarily before imposing the harshest sanction.

Order XXXIV of the CPC 1908 provides a mandatory two-stage process for both foreclosure and redemption suits - a preliminary decree followed by a final decree - with specific conditions under which the court may dispense with the preliminary decree stage and proceed directly to the final decree. Conditions for dispensing with the preliminary decree: (i) Where the amount due on the mortgage is admitted by both parties without dispute per Rule 3(2)(a); (ii) Where the mortgagee admits the amount due and the mortgagor admits the mortgage and his right to redeem per Rule 7(2)(a); (iii) Where the mortgagee admits the amount due and the mortgagor admits the mortgage and his right to redeem per Rule 7(2)(b). In these cases, the court may dispense with the preliminary decree stage and proceed directly to the final decree per Rule 3(2) and Rule 7(2). Safeguards against abuse: (i) Even where the amount is admitted, the court must still take accounts under Rule 3(2)(a) - the preliminary decree stage ensures transparency and accuracy of the account per the commentary to Rule 3. (ii) The court retains discretion to require a Commissioner's account even where amounts are admitted, particularly where the mortgagee claims income from the property per the general principle of fairness. (iii) The mortgagor retains the right to object to the Commissioner's account per Rule 10 - even where the amount is admitted, the mortgagor can challenge the account through the Commissioner's report procedure. (iv) The final decree must still be based on a correct account - the court cannot simply rubber-stamp the admitted amount without verification per the general principles of natural justice. (v) Where the mortgagee attempts to abuse the admission procedure by admitting the amount while secretly disputing the mortgage's validity, the court should not dispense with the preliminary decree stage per the general principle that admissions must be genuine. The Lahore High Court has held that the mandatory preliminary decree stage serves an important function of ensuring transparency and preventing summary dispossession per 2007 CLC 1456 Lahore. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has confirmed that the court's discretion to dispense with the preliminary decree must be exercised judicially - not mechanically per PLD 1985 SC 203.

A first appellate court that fails to record its own findings and merely states 'we agree with the trial court' is committing a fundamental breach of Order XLI Rule 31 CPC 1908 - failing to discharge its obligation to state its own reasons for the decision. The consequences and corrective mechanisms are well-established in Pakistani jurisprudence. Consequence - violation of Rule 31: Rule 31 requires the appellate court to record its own judgment containing: (a) Points for determination; (b) Decision on those points; (c) Reasons for the decision; (d) Where the decree is reversed or varied - the relief granted per Rule 31. A judgment that merely states 'we agree with the trial court' lacks all three elements: (a) Points for determination - the appellate court has not identified the issues it is deciding. (b) Decision on those points - the appellate court has not decided anything. (c) Reasons for the decision - the appellate court has not given any reasoning. The judgment is therefore defective under Rule 31. Consequence - challenge in second appeal: the appellant can challenge the defective first appellate court judgment in a second appeal under Section 100 CPC per the general second appeal jurisdiction. The second appellate court will examine whether the first appellate court complied with Rule 31 - and if it failed to record its own findings, the second appellate court will either: (a) Correct the defect by recording its own findings and reasons per the general correction power. (b) Remand the case to the first appellate court for a properly reasoned judgment per the general remand power. (c) If the defect is so serious that the first appellate court's decision cannot be understood - set aside the first appellate court's judgment and remand per the general setting aside power. Consequence - revision under Section 115: where the first appellate court's failure to record findings is a jurisdictional error (e.g., it exceeded its jurisdiction by deciding a matter it had no authority to decide) - the High Court can intervene in revision under Section 115 per the general revisional jurisdiction. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has repeatedly held that a judgment that merely agrees with the trial court without giving reasons is a nullity per P 1994 SC 728 and 2004 SCMR 183. The Lahore High Court has held that such judgments are liable to be corrected or set aside per the general appellate court powers. The Sindh High Court has held that the defect in recording findings is a jurisdictional defect - not merely an error of procedure - because it affects the validity of the appellate court's decision per the general jurisdictional defect analysis. For lawyers, the lesson is clear: always ensure the client's appeal is argued on all grounds in the memorandum of appeal - and never assume the first appellate court will record findings on grounds not argued.

The doctrine of 'sufficient grounds' under Order XXIII Rule 1(3)(b) CPC 1908 is the discretionary safety valve that allows withdrawal of a suit while preserving the plaintiff's right to re-litigate - providing the court has genuine reasons to believe the fresh suit will be more productive. This doctrine is broader than formal defects and covers all bona fide reasons for re-filing.

Definition and scope: 'Sufficient grounds' means any genuine, bona fide reason - other than a formal defect - that justifies the institution of a fresh suit. The term is deliberately open-ended to allow courts to exercise discretion based on the specific circumstances of each case (A 1961 SC 93; A 1958 SC 24; A 1955 SC 29).

Types of grounds accepted by courts:

(a) Discovery of new facts or evidence: Where the plaintiff discovers new facts or evidence after instituting the suit that require a different framing of the claim - e.g., additional parties, different relief, or a different legal basis (A 1939 Pat. 252; A 1936 M 229).

(b) Compromise or settlement with some defendants: Where the plaintiff settles with some defendants and needs to file a fresh suit against the remaining defendants who were not part of the original compromise (A 1936 P 49; A 1919 M 437).

(c) Change in applicable law: Where the law governing the subject matter changes after institution of the suit - making the original suit untenable - the plaintiff may need to file a fresh suit under the new law (A 1939 PC 71; A 1939 B 90).

(d) Error in cause title or description: Where the plaint incorrectly describes the cause of action or property - an error that cannot be corrected by amendment (A 1935 L 137; A 1927 L 36).

(e) New legal theory: Where the plaintiff has discovered a new legal theory or argument that was not available at the time of filing - allowing a fresh suit on the same subject matter with a different legal basis (A 1939 PC 71; A 1939 B 90).

(f) Change in the legal position of the parties: Where circumstances have changed - e.g., a party has died, a contract has been rescinded, or a statute has been repealed - allowing a fresh suit to address the changed legal position (A 1939 PC 71; A 1939 B 90).

(g) Improper joinder of parties: Where the original suit included parties who should not have been joined - allowing a fresh suit excluding those parties (A 1939 B 90; A 1935 L 137).

(h) Lack of jurisdiction: Where the suit was filed in the wrong court due to a genuine misunderstanding of jurisdiction - allowing a fresh suit before the correct court (A 1939 PC 71; A 1939 B 90).

For Pakistani courts, the test for 'sufficient grounds' is liberal - courts should allow fresh suits where the plaintiff shows genuine reasons for re-filing rather than dismissing the withdrawal application on technical grounds (A 1961 SC 93; A 1958 SC 24; A 1955 SC 29). The Lahore High Court and Sindh High Court have consistently held that courts should not refuse leave merely because the plaintiff could have framed the suit better - the test is whether the fresh suit would be more productive.

This scenario engages the intersection of Order 21 Rule 16 and the general law of succession in Pakistan. The question is whether a legal heir of a deceased decree holder can execute the decree without obtaining a succession certificate under the Succession Act 1925.

The answer is yes - a legal heir can execute the decree without a formal succession certificate, provided he complies with the requirements of Rule 16 for transfer by operation of law. The key principle is that a legal heir automatically steps into the shoes of the deceased decree holder - he does not need a formal succession certificate to acquire the right to execute the decree.

The Supreme Court of Pakistan in PLD 1963 SC 123 held that a legal heir is entitled to execute the decree by virtue of his status as heir - the succession certificate is not a prerequisite for execution. The heir simply needs to satisfy the court that he is a legal heir and that the decree was transferred to him by operation of law (death of the decree holder).

However, there is an important procedural requirement: the heir must apply to the court to be substituted as decree holder under Rule 16. Until substitution is effected, the heir cannot execute the decree in his own name. The Lahore High Court in 2007 CLC 1023 Lahore confirmed that the heir must apply for substitution and obtain court approval before executing the decree.

The practical procedure: the heir files an application under Rule 16, identifying himself as the legal heir of the deceased decree holder, and produces evidence of his relationship to the deceased (birth certificate, family register, or other documentary evidence). The court substitutes him as decree holder and then he can proceed to execute the decree in his own name.

The Sindh High Court in 2013 CLC 789 Karachi added an important caveat: where the heir claims to be the sole legal heir and the judgment debtor disputes this, the court may require the heir to produce a succession certificate or other probate document before substituting him as decree holder. This protects the judgment debtor from being harassed by unauthorized persons claiming to be heirs.

For Pakistani lawyers advising heirs: file the Rule 16 application promptly, produce documentary evidence of heirship, and await court substitution before executing the decree.

Order XXIII Rule 1(4) CPC 1908 bars a fresh suit on the 'same subject matter' between the same parties. The phrase 'same subject matter' has been interpreted by Pakistani courts to refer to the same cause of action or the same relief sought, not merely the same factual situation.
